name: Perchta
description: Frau Perchta (also Berchta, 'the Bright One') is a powerful winter goddess and guardian of moral order in Alpine Germanic folklore, widely regarded as the southern equivalent of Frau Holle. She belongs to the pre-Christian pantheon of continental Germanic peoples and was once venerated as a white-robed deity who oversaw spinning, weaving, and the domestic virtues. During the twelve Rauhnächte (Rough Nights) between Christmas and Epiphany, Perchta roams the countryside entering homes to judge the behavior of children and servants throughout the year. She rewards the industrious with a small silver coin, but the lazy and disobedient face horrific punishment: she slits open their bellies and stuffs the cavity with straw and stones. Her particular concern is spinning — girls who leave their flax unspun by Twelfth Night face her wrath. Despite Church efforts to demonize her (Luther himself railed against 'Fraw Hulde'), Perchta survives in Alpine Perchtenläufe — processions of Schönperchten and Schiachperchten that continue to this day In Germany folklore, this figure is known among the Germany people.
source: Alpine folklore; Frau Perchta is a powerful winter goddess and guardian of domestic order.

name: Peri
description: Peri are beautiful winged supernatural beings in Azerbaijani folklore, derived from Persian mythology and deeply integrated into Turkic folk tradition. These enchanting spirits are morally ambivalent but predominantly benevolent, often helping humans in distress and guiding heroes on quests. Peris live in elaborate underground kingdoms with gardens and palaces, organized into societies mirroring human structure. They frequently appear as white doves or gazelles bathing at springs, shedding their animal skins to reveal stunning human forms. If a man steals a Peri's feather garment or animal skin while she bathes, she may be bound to him and can be married. Peris are locked in eternal conflict with their malevolent counterparts, the Divs. They appear throughout the Kitabi-Dede Korkut tales and Azerbaijani fairy tales like 'Malikmammad'
source: Persianate Afghan folklore — Peri spirit beings.

name: Peri
description: Peri are beautiful winged supernatural beings in Azerbaijani folklore, derived from Persian mythology and deeply integrated into Turkic folk tradition. These enchanting spirits are morally ambivalent but predominantly benevolent, often helping humans in distress and guiding heroes on quests. Peris live in elaborate underground kingdoms with gardens and palaces, organized into societies mirroring human structure. If a man steals a Peri's feather garment or animal skin while she bathes, she may be bound to him and can be married. Peris are locked in eternal conflict with their malevolent counterparts, the Divs. They appear throughout the Kitabi-Dede Korkut tales and Azerbaijani fairy tales like 'Malikmammad' In Azerbaijan folklore, this figure is known among the Azerbaijan people.
source: Azerbaijani/Persian folklore; Peri are winged supernatural beings.

name: Phaya Thaen (Sky God)
description: Phaya Thaen (Lao: ພະຍາແຖນ, also known as Phi Thaen or Phi Fa) is the supreme sky god and creator deity in traditional Lao and Tai folk religion. He is the highest celestial being who rules over heaven (Muang Fa) and is responsible for sending rain, creating the world, and appointing kings. According to the Nithan Khun Borom chronicle, Phaya Thaen destroyed the corrupt first humanity with a great flood, sparing only three righteous chiefs. When they returned to earth, he sent a buffalo to help them cultivate; after the buffalo died, gourds grew and produced the new human races. He then sent his son Khun Borom to rule as the first king. Phaya Thaen controls rain and weather — the annual Bun Bang Fai (Rocket Festival) is performed to signal him to send rain. In Lao Buddhist cosmology, he was syncretized with Indra/Sakra, but retains his distinct identity as the primordial creator in folk practice. His name derives from 'thae' meaning 'truth' or 'real' — making him 'the Lord of Truth.'
source: Lao oral tradition, Tai folk religion, Nithan Khun Borom chronicles

name: Nang Phisuea Samud (Sea Ogress)
description: Nang Phisuea Samud (Thai: นางผีเสื้อสมุทร) is a powerful sea ogress from the Thai national epic Phra Aphai Mani by Sunthorn Phu. She is a giant ogress of the deep ocean who kidnapped Prince Aphai Mani after hearing his enchanted flute playing. Despite her terrifying appearance as a sea monster, she fell deeply in love with the prince and kept him imprisoned in her undersea cave palace for eight years. During this time, she bore him a son named Sin Samudr. The story explores themes of love across boundaries — the ogress loves genuinely but cannot overcome her predatory nature. She was ultimately killed by Aphai Mani's flute magic when she attacked the island where he had taken refuge. Nang Phisuea Samud represents the complex portrayal of non-human beings in Thai literature: monstrous yet capable of deep emotion, loving yet ultimately destructive
source: Sunthorn Phu's Phra Aphai Mani epic (1822-1844 CE)

name: Sea Beast of Raouche
description: The Sea Beast of Raouche is a legendary monster from Lebanese coastal folklore associated with the famous Pigeon Rocks (Raouche) off the coast of Beirut. According to local legend, a fearsome sea monster once threatened the land around Raouche, demanding human sacrifices from the terrified locals. To appease the beast, the people chose to sacrifice the beautiful princess Andromeda. Before the sacrifice could be completed, the hero Perseus arrived, bringing with him the severed head of Medusa. In an epic battle on the coast, Perseus deployed Medusa's petrifying gaze, turning the monstrous sea beast permanently to stone. The Pigeon Rocks that stand today off Beirut's coast are said to be the petrified remains of the monster, weathered by centuries of sea and stone. This legend blends Greek mythology with local Lebanese geography
source: Beirut.com; Lebanese oral coastal traditions; Greek mythological adaptation

name: Pishacha (Flesh-Eating Demon)
description: Pishachas are flesh-eating demons in Indian religions, appearing in Hindu and Buddhist traditions as malevolent beings often referred to as the very manifestation of evil. According to the Mahabharata, they were created by Brahma, and other legends describe them as sons of Krodha (Anger) or as descendants of Kashyapa and Krodhavasa. They are described as having bulging veins and protruding red eyes. Pishachas haunt cremation grounds along with other monsters like bhutas and vetālas. They possess the ability to shapeshift, become invisible, and feed on human energy. They can possess human beings and alter their thoughts, causing insanity and various maladies. Certain mantras and rituals are prescribed to cure those afflicted by pishacha possession. When burial or funeral rites are not performed properly, the deceased's soul may become trapped in the corpse and transform into a pishacha — unable to eat or drink, blind, and suffering immensely, yet instinctively craving the living
source: Mahabharata, Nilamata Purana, Kathasaritsagara, Hindu and Buddhist traditions

name: Popa Medaw (Mother of Mount Popa)
description: Popa Medaw (Burmese: ပုပ္ပားမယ်တော်, 'Royal Mother of Popa') is the most important female nat in the Burmese pantheon, the mother of all nats who presides over Mount Popa, an extinct volcano in central Myanmar. According to legend, she was the sister of the blacksmith Nga Tin De (who became the Mahagiri Nat). When King Thinligyawng of Tagaung burned her brother alive in a champaca tree out of fear, she threw herself into the flames to die beside him. Their spirits became trapped in the tree until King Anawrahta had the tree cut down and the spirits carved into statues. Popa Medaw was enshrined on Mount Popa, which became the most important nat pilgrimage site in Myanmar. She is the protector of women, children, and families, and is also associated with flowers, beauty, and prosperity. Her shrine on Mount Popa receives thousands of pilgrims annually, especially women seeking blessings for fertility and family harmony
source: Burmese nat religion — Popa Medaw mother spirit of Mount Popa.

name: Preah Keo (Sacred Gem)
description: Preah Keo (Khmer: ព្រះកែវ, 'Sacred Gem') is the younger brother in the famous Khmer folktale of Preah Ko and Preah Keo. Born under a shining gem that foretold his magical destiny, Preah Keo possessed supernatural powers and wisdom beyond his years. Together with his elder brother Preah Ko (born under a sacred ox), he embarked on adventures encountering giants, rescuing princesses, and overcoming enchantments. While Preah Ko represented physical strength and virtue, Preah Keo contributed magical insight, spiritual wisdom, and strategic thinking. The legend teaches that the balance of earthly strength and spiritual wisdom creates complete virtue. The 'gem' of his name symbolizes the inner light of knowledge and enlightenment. The story remains central to Cambodian shadow puppet theater (sbek thom) and classical dance traditions, performed at festivals and ceremonies throughout the country
source: Cambodian Khmer folklore — Preah Keo sacred figure.

name: Preah Ko (Sacred Ox)
description: Preah Ko (Khmer: ព្រះគោ, 'Sacred Ox') is a legendary sacred ox from one of Cambodia's most beloved folktales. The story follows two orphaned brothers — the elder Preah Ko (born under a sacred ox) and the younger Preah Keo (born under a shining gem). Preah Ko grew to be strong and virtuous, while Preah Keo possessed magical powers. Their adventures tested their complementary strengths — Preah Ko's physical fortitude and Preah Keo's magical insight. The sacred ox represents Preah Ko's humble origins and his connection to agriculture and labor. The temple of Preah Ko at Roluos (built by King Indravarman I in the 9th century) is named after this legend, with its three towers dedicated to the king's ancestors. The ox is also linked to the Hindu Nandi (Shiva's mount) through Khmer adaptation, giving it a dual significance in both folk religion and the Hindu-Buddhist temple tradition
source: Cambodian Khmer folklore — Preah Ko sacred bull/cow.

name: Preah Thaong (Kaundinya I)
description: Preah Thaong (also known as Kaundinya I) is the legendary Brahmin prince from India who founded the Kingdom of Funan, the earliest known Cambodian state, in the 1st century CE. According to the foundational Khmer creation myth, Preah Thong received a divine instruction in a dream to take a magic bow and sail east. He arrived on the coast of what is now Cambodia, where he encountered the Naga princess Neang Neak (Queen Soma) — daughter of the Naga serpent king. After shooting a magic arrow from his bow, the princess agreed to marry him. Her father, the Naga king, drank the ocean waters to reveal land for their kingdom, creating the Cambodian heartland. Their marriage united Indian and indigenous Khmer cultures — introducing Brahmanic traditions, Sanskrit, and Hindu governance — while the Naga heritage provided spiritual legitimacy. Preah Thong symbolizes the foreign element that blended with native traditions to create Khmer civilization. He is considered the founder of the royal dynasty that ruled Cambodia for nearly 2,000 years
source: Khmer royal chronicles, Chinese historical records (Kang Tai, Zhu Ying)

name: Prince Sattva (Mahasattva Jataka)
description: Prince Sattva (also known as Prince Mahasattva) is the Bodhisattva in one of the most famous Jataka tales — the story of the starving tigress, from the Jataka-mala (Garland of Birth Stories) by Aryasura. In this past life, the future Buddha was born as Prince Sattva, the youngest son of a king. While wandering in the forest with his two elder brothers, they discovered a starving tigress near a mountain gorge. The tigress was so weak from hunger that she could not nurse her newborn cubs and was on the verge of eating them out of desperation. Overwhelmed with compassion, Prince Sattva sent his brothers ahead on a pretext, then lay down before the tigress to offer his body. When the tigress was too weak even to bite him, the prince cut his throat with a sharp bamboo stick. The scent of blood revived the tigress, who ate his flesh, saving both her and her cubs. His brothers returned to find only his bones. The prince attained a higher spiritual state through this act of ultimate generosity (dana paramita), and his relics were enshrined in a stupa that the Buddha later pointed out to his disciples
source: Aryasura's Jatakamala (Garland of Birth Stories), Pali Jataka commentary

name: Puteri Gunung Ledang (Princess of Mount Ledang)
description: Puteri Gunung Ledang is a celestial princess and guardian spirit of Mount Ledang (Mount Ophir) in Johor, Malaysia. According to legend, the powerful Sultan of Melaka, Sultan Mahmud Shah, heard of her legendary beauty and sought her hand in marriage. The princess agreed — but only if the Sultan fulfilled seven impossible conditions: build a golden bridge from Melaka to the mountain, build a silver bridge back, provide seven trays of mosquito hearts, a vat of virgin's tears, a bowl of his son's blood, and two cups each of the Sultan's own blood and semen. The Sultan fulfilled six conditions but hesitated at the final ones, realizing the princess never intended to marry him. The princess is considered a guardian spirit of the mountain, appearing only to those pure of heart, and her legend is a timeless lesson in humility and the folly of pride
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legend_of_Puteri_Gunung_Ledang

name: Quetzalcoatl
description: THE FEATHERED SERPENT — the most important syncretic deity in Mexican and Mexican-American spiritual folklore. In Aztec tradition, Quetzalcóatl was the god of wind (Ehecatl), knowledge, learning, the priesthood, and the morning star (Venus). He is credited with creating humanity by descending to Mictlan (the underworld) and mixing his own blood with the bones of previous generations to create a new race of people. He is the inventor of books, the calendar, and the arts of civilization. The feathered serpent iconography appears throughout Mesoamerica from Teotihuacan (200 BCE) to the Aztec Empire, with his worship centered at Cholula's great pyramid — the largest pyramid by volume in the world. Quetzalcóatl's name combines 'quetzal' (the brilliant green bird) and 'coatl' (serpent), symbolizing the union of earth and sky. In one of his most famous myths, he was tricked by Tezcatlipoca into getting drunk and sleeping with his sister, leading to his exile — but he promised to return from the east. This prophesied return was later fatally conflated with Hernán Cortés's arrival in 1519, a complex historical narrative that continues to shape Mexican-American understanding of conquest and cultural survival. In Chicano spirituality, Quetzalcóatl has been reclaimed as a powerful symbol of indigenous identity, cultural resistance, and the profound wisdom of pre-Columbian civilizations
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Qutrub
description: The Qutrub (also spelled Qutrub) is a type of werehyena from Arabian folklore, a shape-shifting creature that combines human and hyena traits. According to the 10th-century scholar al-Mas'udi, the Qutrub was created from a split egg of a female jinn — its counterpart being the Marid (powerful sea jinn). The Qutrub is described as resembling a cat-like creature that haunts graveyards, eating corpses. Pre-Islamic Arabs considered the Qutrub a type of jinn or demon closely associated with death and transformation. Like the European werewolf but with a hyena as its base form, the Qutrub can shift between human and animal form at night. The hyena's scavenging habits, unsettling calls that resemble human laughter, and presence near burial grounds made it a natural candidate for a creature associated with death and deception. The Qutrub is less known than the Ghul but represents an important strand of Arabian shapeshifter mythology tied to specific animals
source: Al-Mas'udi, Muruj al-Dhahab (Meadows of Gold); al-Jahiz; Fee, Mythology in the Middle Ages

name: Rørosgubben
description: Rørosgubben (the Old Man of Røros) is a ghostly miner said to haunt the Røros Copper Works and the surrounding mining areas in the Røros region of Trøndelag. Røros was one of Norway's most important mining towns from its founding in 1644 until the mines closed in 1977. The ghost is believed to be the spirit of a miner who died in a cave-in or accident, and who now roams the tunnels, surface works, and slag heaps. The Rørosgubben is said to appear before disasters, warning miners of impending cave-ins, gas leaks, or other dangers. He is also seen walking through the characteristic black-timbered streets of Røros town. Some versions say he is searching for a lost treasure he hid before his death, while others claim he is a protective spirit who watches over the miners and their families. The legend is well known among the Røros community and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site's cultural heritage
source: Norwegian folklore; Rørosgubben is a ghostly miner from the Røros Copper Works.

name: Radien-attje
description: Radien-attje (also Raedie or Veralden Olmai, meaning 'World Man') is the supreme high god in Sami mythology, the ruler of the cosmos and the celestial father. He is the creator and giver of life, sitting at the head of the divine family trinity alongside his wife Raedieahkka and their son Radien-pardne. In some traditions their daughter Rana Niejta is also included. He is more of an intellectual superior who maintains cosmic order rather than interfering directly — his son Radien-pardne performs practical tasks. His name derives from Old Norse 'ráð' meaning 'rule, governance.' Every autumn, the Sami erected a sacrificial pole symbolizing the world-pillar (Veralden stytto) that connects the earth to the Pole Star, to honor him and prevent the pillar's collapse. He creates human souls and hands them to Máttaráhkká who gives them life. He also takes the souls of the dead back to himself. Some scholars argue that Radien-attje was a later addition to Sami religion, formed from Norse and early Christian influences, while the eastern Sami thunder god Tiermes may have been the original sky god
source: Wikipedia (Radien-attje); saamelaisensyklopedia.fi; babilim.info

name: Raedieahkka
description: Raedieahkka (also Radien-akka) is the supreme goddess in Sami mythology, the wife of the high god Radien-attje. Together with her husband, she created the world and the human soul — they are described as the two divinities who jointly created the cosmos. She is the mother of Rana Niejta (the spring goddess) and Radien-pardne (the son who executes his father's will). She forms part of the Sami divine trinity alongside her husband and son. In some traditions, this trinity reflects Christian influence (Father, Mother, Son replacing Father, Son, Holy Spirit), but the concept of a divine couple creating the world together is deeply rooted in Finno-Ugric tradition. Her role in creation of the human soul places her at the very beginning of existence alongside Radien-attje, before the soul is passed to Máttaráhkká and her daughters who handle gestation and birth
source: Wikipedia (Raedieahkka); saamelaisensyklopedia.fi; everything.explained.today

name: Rana Niejta
description: Rana Niejta is the Sami spring and vegetation goddess, the daughter of the high god Radien-attje and his wife Raedieahkka. Her name means 'the green' or 'the fertile fields.' She makes the southern slopes of mountains turn green so hungry reindeer have food after the long Arctic winter. She is one of three divine sisters who together control the seasonal cycle: Sala Niejta (Sun's daughter) ends winter's cold, Rana Niejta brings forth vegetation, and Saivo Niejta governs the underworld. She belongs to the Radien family of spirits — a group of deities who had power over human lives. A bronze statue of Rana Niejta stands in Mo i Rana, Norway, a town whose name some scholars connect to the goddess. Her figure on Sami drums connects her to the fertility of the earth and the prosperity of the reindeer herds
source: Wikipedia (Rana Niejta); beneathnorthernlights.com; baalka.se

name: Rannamaari (Sea Demon of the Maldives)
description: Rannamaari is a terrifying sea demon from Maldivian folklore that rose from the ocean each month to demand a sacrifice of a virgin girl. According to legend, before the Islamization of the Maldives in 1153 CE, the Buddhist inhabitants of Malé were terrorized by this demon. Each month, a virgin was dressed in fine clothes and left alone overnight in a temple on the eastern seafront of Malé — by dawn, she was found violated and dead. This practice continued until a Maghrebi Muslim traveler, Abu'l-Barakat al-Barbari (alternatively identified as Yusuf al-Tabrezi from Tabriz, Iran), arrived in the islands. Outraged by the practice, he volunteered to take the girl's place. He spent the night reciting the Quran, and when the demon appeared, the power of the holy verses caused it to flee into the sea, never to return. The king, identified as Dhovemi, was so moved that he converted to Islam along with his court, taking the name Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah. Folklorist Xavier Romero-Frias traces the name Rannamaari to a South Indian goddess, suggesting a pre-Islamic Hindu-Buddhist origin for the belief
source: Ibn Battuta travelogue (14th century), Isdhoo Loamaafaanu copper plates, Xavier Romero-Frias research

name: Rauðkembingur
description: Rauðkembingur (Red-Crest) is the most savage of all the illhveli (evil whales) in Icelandic folklore. It has a distinctive red crest or mane running along its back and is 10-20 meters long, streamlined, and extremely fast in the water. Rauðkembingur attacks ships with unmatched ferocity, ramming them at high speed and leaping across decks. It neighs ominously before attacking. According to one legend, a callous young man was cursed by elves into becoming a rauðkembingur as punishment for his cruelty. The rauðkembingur was considered one of the most dangerous creatures in Icelandic waters, feared even more than the larger illhveli because of its speed and aggression. The name comes from rauður (red) and kembingur (crest/mane). The tradition likely originated from sightings of killer whales (orca), which have distinctive white patches that could be interpreted as a crest
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Rávga
description: Rávga (from Norse 'draug') is an undead sea creature in Sami folklore — the soul of a drowned person whose body was never found and properly buried. Unlike the Čáhcerávga (water wraith) which was known to be fictional, the Rávga was believed to be real and dangerous. It appears as a long-haired, large-mouthed creature in human form that harasses sailors and people on shore. It calls out and imitates the speech of the living to lure people to their deaths or simply frighten them. It can be driven away by reading the funeral service to it — this releases it from its undead state. The Rávga is not truly malevolent in the way of demons but is displaced and uneasy due to its unresolved death. It illustrates the Sami concern with proper burial and the danger of souls that have not been transitioned correctly to the afterlife. The legend is concentrated in coastal Sami areas of Norway and Finland
source: saamelaisensyklopedia.fi (Rávga); Qvigstad collection; Sami Folktales from the Near and Far Worlds

name: Riri Yaksha (Blood Demon of Sri Lanka)
description: Riri Yaksha (Blood Demon) is one of the most feared demonic figures in Sinhalese folklore, central to the Bali and Tovil exorcism traditions of Sri Lanka. According to legend, Riri Yaksha was born from the blood of a slain demon — when a powerful demon was killed, his spilled blood gave rise to this new, even more malevolent entity. He possesses enormous power and an insatiable thirst for blood and destruction. Unlike other disease demons who cause specific ailments, Riri Yaksha is associated with general misfortune, madness, violent death, and uncontrollable rage. He is considered one of the most dangerous of the demonic hierarchy, requiring the most powerful exorcism rituals to subdue. The Tovil ritual performed against Riri Yaksha involves elaborate masks painted predominantly red (symbolizing blood), intense drumming, acrobatic dancing, and the recitation of potent protective chants (paritta). In some traditions, Riri Yaksha is associated with untimely or violent deaths — those who die in accidents, murders, or battles are at risk of being transformed into his minions
source: Sinhalese Tovil exorcism traditions, Gananath Obeyesekere 'Medusa's Hair', Sinhala folk Buddhism

name: Roro Jonggrang (Slender Maiden)
description: Roro Jonggrang is the tragic princess at the heart of the Javanese legend explaining the origin of Prambanan Temple. When the powerful prince Bandung Bondowoso fell in love with her and she rejected him, he attacked and conquered her father's kingdom. Forced to consider marriage, Roro Jonggrang set an impossible condition: Bandung must build 1,000 temples in one night. Using his supernatural army of invisible spirits (jin), he nearly completed the task. Desperate, Roro Jonggrang ordered her maids to light fires and pound rice, tricking the spirits into thinking dawn had arrived. Enraged by the deception, Bandung cursed Roro Jonggrang, transforming her into stone — the 1,000th statue that completes the temple count. Her stone form remains at Prambanan to this day as the temple's central Durga statue
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roro_Jonggrang

name: Rounce
description: The Rounce is a unique figure from Vincentian folklore — a guardian spirit of the natural world that is specific to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. The Rounce is believed to be a nature spirit that dwells in the dense forests and mountains of the island, serving as a protector of the land and its creatures. Vincentians tell stories of the Rounce appearing to those who venture too deep into the forest or who disrespect the natural environment. The creature is elusive and rarely seen, but its presence is felt through sudden changes in the weather, strange sounds in the bush, or the feeling of being watched. The Rounce legend reflects Saint Vincent's rich blending of African, Kalinago/Garifuna, and French Creole spiritual traditions. Like Papa Bois in other islands, the Rounce teaches respect for nature and the consequences of environmental destruction
source: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines oral tradition; snip Vincentian folklore collections

name: Sømunk
description: Sømunken (the Sea Monk) is a sea monster reportedly caught in the Øresund in 1546 and presented to King Christian III of Denmark. The creature was described in contemporary sources as being four ells long (approximately 2.5 meters), shaped like a fish but with a monk-like head featuring a tonsure and a body resembling a monk's robe. It was kept alive in the Copenhagen castle moat for three days before dying, after which it was given a Christian burial. This historical event was documented in natural history texts of the 16th century, including Conrad Gesner's Historiae Animalium (1558). The creature was retrospectively identified in 1854 by Danish zoologist Japetus Steenstrup as a giant squid (Architeuthis), which would explain the tentacles that witnesses described as the 'monk's robe' and the head shape as seen from certain angles
source: Danish folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Sætrevette
description: Sætrevette (seter wight) is a nature spirit that guards the mountain pastures and seter huts in Vestlandet. The sætrevette protects the cattle, goats, and sheep taken to the summer pastures in the high mountains. Every seter (summer mountain farm) had its own sætrevette who ensured the animals were healthy, the milk yield was good, and the cheese-making succeeded. The sætrevette could appear as a small grey woman, a beautiful girl, or an old man. She would help with the milking and cheese-making if treated respectfully, but would sour the milk, hide the cheese curds, or lead the cattle astray if offended. Offerings of the first cheese of the season were left in the seter hut. The sætrevette tradition was particularly strong in the seter pastures of Vestlandet — Hallingdal, Valdres, Jotunheimen, and Hardangervidda. The seter system was central to Norwegian dairy farming, and the sætrevette was its supernatural guardian
source: Scandinavian folklore; Vættir are nature spirits of the land and water.

name: Sacred Drum Spirit
description: The Sacred Drum (Ngoma ya Bulopwe) is a legendary spirit-imbued royal drum in Luba tradition, believed to contain the soul of the Luba nation. According to tradition, the first sacred drum was given by the spirit of the forest, its voice carrying the power of ancestors. The drum's beat could be heard across the entire kingdom, announcing the king's health, war, or death of a ruler. Luba kings kept the sacred drum in a special house guarded by initiated priests. It was played only during coronations, royal funerals, and times of crisis. Its rhythm was coded language understood by the initiated. The drum was often carved with a female figure, as women were believed to mediate between kings and the spirit world. When the Belgians colonized the Congo, the last sacred drum was hidden in the forest, where some say it still beats
source: Luba oral tradition, Central African folklore, Hamill Gallery

name: Saharan Desert Jinn (Jenun)
description: In Mauritania, belief in desert jinn (locally called jenun) is deeply embedded in the culture, shaped by the vast and unforgiving Saharan landscape. Mauritanian jinn are supernatural beings made of smokeless fire who inhabit the empty deserts, ancient ruins, oases, and remote mountain passes of this largely desert nation. The harsh Sahara creates a unique spiritual landscape where natural phenomena like sandstorms, mirages, and the howling of desert winds are attributed to jinn activity. Mauritanian folklore distinguishes between different types of jinn: some are Muslim and harmless, while others are unbelieving and malevolent. The desert jinn are particularly associated with the hours of darkness, when travelers may hear their voices carried on the wind or see their fires flickering in the distance. Tales of people being led astray by jinn who disguise themselves as fellow travelers are common. The concept of the 'evil eye' and jinn possession is also prevalent, with traditional healers (fqihs) using Quranic verses and incense to provide protection and treatment
source: Mexicohistorico.com; Saharan oral traditions

name: Salu'ah
description: The Salu'ah (feminine grammatical form, as opposed to Salu — masculine) is the Arabian she-wolf, a monstrous creature from Bedouin folklore of northern Saudi Arabia. According to Bedouin oral traditions collected by Fatmah Alblui in her anthology 'Salu'ah: Between Fact and Fantasy,' the Salu'ah is a hairy, ugly animal-like woman who hunts primarily men and occasionally children and women. She has sharp teeth, howls like a wolf, and can transform herself into an old woman to approach unsuspecting victims. Unlike the more generic Ghul, the Salu'ah is specifically a monstrous feminine figure — representing the inversion of traditional gender roles. The Bedouins had an ambivalent relationship with wolves, respecting their hunting abilities while fearing their attacks. The Salu'ah myth served to explain disappearances in the desert and reinforce social norms. She represents the terrifying power of female agency in a patriarchal society, the 'monstrous feminine' that devours men rather than serving them
source: Alblui, Salu'ah: Between Fact and Fantasy (2011); Hanan Alazaz, 'Salu'ah: The She-Wolf of Arabia' (Lancaster University); Jabbur, The Bedouins

name: Saman Deviyo (Guardian of Adam's Peak)
description: Saman Deviyo (also known as Sumana Saman) is one of the four guardian deities (Catura Varam Deviyo) of Sri Lanka in Sinhalese Buddhist tradition. He is the divine protector of Adam's Peak (Sri Pada), the sacred mountain that is one of the most important pilgrimage sites in Sri Lanka. According to the Mahavamsa, the Buddha, on his deathbed, entrusted the care of Lanka to the god Sumana, who later appeared to Prince Vijaya's followers disguised as a wandering ascetic. Saman is associated with the Sumana Saman mountain range and is considered the guardian of the Buddha's footprint atop Adam's Peak — a footprint revered by Buddhists (as Buddha's), Hindus (as Shiva's), Muslims (as Adam's), and Christians (as St. He is often depicted as a regal figure riding an elephant, holding a lotus flower, and wearing royal white garments. He is considered the most prominent of the guardian deities and is invoked first in most Sinhalese Buddhist rituals. His principal shrine is at Ratnapura, where the Saman Devalaya (shrine) houses his image and receives offerings from pilgrims before they begin their climb
source: Mahavamsa, Sinhala Buddhist traditions, Adam's Peak pilgrimage traditions

name: Santa Muerte
aliases: Nuestra Señora de la Santa Muerte
description: Santa Muerte (Holy Death) is a female folk saint and personification of death venerated primarily in Mexico and the US Southwest, with an estimated 12 million followers worldwide. She is depicted as a female skeleton wearing a long robe and carrying a scythe and a globe. Her origins blend pre-Columbian death deities such as the Aztec goddess Mictēcacihuātl (Lady of the Dead) with the Spanish Grim Reaper (la Parca). Devotees pray to Santa Muerte for protection, healing, financial prosperity, love, and safe passage to the afterlife. Her statues are dressed in different colored robes: white for purification, red for love, gold for money, black for protection against enemies, green for justice. Though condemned by the Catholic Church, her following exploded in the early 2000s and spread rapidly to the United States through Mexican immigration. She is the center of the fastest-growing new religious movement in the Americas, with shrines found throughout Los Angeles, Houston, Chicago, New York, and other cities with large Mexican-American populations. She has particular appeal among those on society's margins — taxi drivers, sex workers, police, soldiers, and prisoners — who face death's uncertainty daily
source: Mexican folk religion — Santa Muerte is the folk saint of death documented in contemporary Mexican tradition.

name: Sáráhkká
description: Sáráhkká is the most important birth goddess in Sami mythology, daughter of Máttaráhkká. She lives under the hearth (aernie) of the goahti (Sami tent). She is the most worshipped of the Sami goddesses of childbirth. When Radien-attje creates a soul and sends it to Máttaráhkká who gives it life, Máttaráhkká hands it to Sáráhkká, who places the fetus in the woman's womb and gives it a body. She protects both human women and reindeer during birth, feeling the same labor pains. Before labor, women drank 'Sáráhkká's booze' and after birth ate 'Sáráhkká's porridge.' Wood was split for her to ease delivery — the split pieces were so sacred no one could touch them. A dog was kept during pregnancy and buried alive at labor time as a sacrifice. After successful birth, a female animal was sacrificed (only female animals except roosters). Her cult was so strong that after Christianization, Sami held secret ceremonies consuming 'the flesh and blood of Sáráhkká' before or after going to church, and she was replaced by the Virgin Mary. The modern Sami women's organization Sarahkka (formed 1988) is named after her
source: Wikipedia (Sáráhkká); baalka.se; Sami shamanism articles

name: Schrat
description: The Schrat (plural Schratln) is a versatile and regionally diverse German legendary creature, appearing as either a wood sprite, a domestic kobold, or a nightmare demon depending on location and tradition. The term is ancient, entering Slavic languages as skrat, skrzat (Polish), skřítek (Czech), and even Estonian kratt — a testament to its deep Indo-European roots. In Bavaria and Austria, the Waldschrat is a solitary forest-dwelling spirit, small and mischievous, who plays malicious pranks on woodcutters and hikers. It breaks their axes, fells trees in wrong directions, and leads travelers astray with mocking laughter. In other regions, particularly the Upper Palatinate, the Schrat is a domestic house spirit akin to a kobold, protecting the home and bringing prosperity if respected, but causing chaos if offended. In Switzerland and the Alemannic regions, the Schratteli is an alp-like nightmare demon that causes sleep paralysis and has a unibrow — the telltale mark of those connected to the spirit world. The Schrat is considered the origin of the English term 'scrat' as an archaic word for a devil or goblin
source: German folklore; the Schrat is a versatile forest spirit in Austrian tradition.

name: Se
description: Se is the concept of divine law, destiny, and cosmic order in Ewe cosmology. Se represents the moral and spiritual foundation of the universe — the divine principles established by Mawu that govern all existence. In Ewe belief, Se is not a personified deity but the underlying law that maintains balance between the spiritual and physical worlds. Se encompasses the rules of ancestral veneration, the moral code that Ewe people must follow, and the destiny assigned to each person. Honoring Se means maintaining proper relationships with the ancestors (through libations and offerings), following ethical conduct, and respecting the natural order. The Ewe believe that violating Se brings misfortune, while living in harmony with it brings blessings. Se is akin to the concept of Ma'at in Egyptian thought or the Yoruba concept of ase
source: Ewe oral tradition of Togo — Se spirit figure.

name: Buku Spirits
description: Buku spirits are powerful and volatile forest-dwelling supernatural beings in the mythology of the Jola (Diola) people of Senegal, particularly in the Casamance region. These spirits inhabit the sacred forests, groves, and wilderness areas that surround Jola villages, acting as both guardians and potential threats. The Buku are deeply feared and revered for their unpredictable nature and for their intimate connection to the mysteries of the bush — the untamed wilderness that exists beyond human settlements. They are associated with initiation rituals, traditional healing, and the maintenance of social order. When properly propitiated, Buku spirits can offer protection, guidance, and fertility to the community. However, if offended through violations of taboos or disrespect to sacred spaces, they can bring illness, misfortune, or even death. The Buku embody the Jola worldview that the natural world is filled with powerful, sentient forces that demand respect and careful negotiation. Their worship involves secret society ceremonies, offerings at sacred groves, and the guidance of ritual specialists who serve as intermediaries
source: Jola oral tradition

name: Faro
description: Faro is a powerful water deity in Mandinka and Bambara (Mandé) mythology, revered across Senegal, Mali, and The Gambia as a purifying force that brings cosmic order, speech, and fertility to the world. In Mandé creation narratives, Faro sacrificed himself to atone for the sins of his twin brother Pemba, being cut into sixty pieces that fell to earth and became trees. The supreme creator Mangala restored Faro to life in human form, sending him to earth in an ark made from his placenta carrying the first ancestors, animals, and plants. Faro then caused a great flood to wash away the impurity created by Pemba, saving only the righteous in his ark. Faro is associated with water purification, spiritual justice, rebirth, and the Niger River, which is considered his physical manifestation. He also granted humanity the gift of speech and language, establishing the foundation of culture and social order. Faro represents the Mandinka concept that true creation requires sacrifice, purification, and the establishment of balance between opposing forces
source: Mandinka/Bambara oral tradition

name: Pangool
description: The Pangool (singular: Fangool) are the ancient saints and ancestral spirits of the Serer people of Senegal, the Gambia, and Mauritania, serving as the central spiritual bridge between humanity and the supreme creator deity Roog. Unlike distant gods, the Pangool are intimately involved in daily life — they are canonized ancestors who have been elevated to spirit status due to their exceptional leadership, sacrifice, or spiritual alignment during their lives. They act as protectors, moral guides, healers, and intermediaries, ensuring balance between human action and cosmic order. The Pangool are associated with specific families, villages, natural features, and sacred geography. Their most recognized symbol is the serpent, often depicted as two coiled snakes, representing spiritual vigilance and continuity. The Serer maintain that the Pangool are not merely historical ancestors but active spiritual forces that respond to proper ritual observance. Sacred groves, ancestral trees, and shrines dedicated to the Pangool continue to be protected across Serer territory, and annual ceremonies invoke their protection during planting seasons and community transitions
source: Wikipedia (Serer religion)

name: Yumboes
description: The Yumboes are supernatural fairy-like beings from the folklore of the Wolof and Lebou people of Senegal, often described as the spirits of the dead. Standing only about two feet tall with pearly-white skin and silver hair, these nocturnal beings live beneath the Paps hills near Gorée Island and emerge to dance in the moonlight. Despite their small stature, the Yumboes are known for hosting elaborate feasts on large tables, waited on by invisible servants whose only visible features are their hands and feet. They are generally benevolent and welcoming, often inviting both natives and foreigners to join their celebrations. The Yumboes are said to eat corn that they steal from humans and fish that they catch themselves. Their name is derived from the Wolof word for 'pumpkin,' reflecting their fondness for stealing human food. The only known source for the Yumboes legend is Thomas Keightley's 1828 book 'The Fairy Mythology,' based on accounts from a woman who lived on Gorée Island as a child and learned of them from a Wolof maid
source: Wolof/Lebou oral tradition, documented by Thomas Keightley

name: Seri Gumum (Dragon of Tasik Chini)
description: Seri Gumum is a legendary dragon (naga) said to dwell in the depths of Tasik Chini (Chini Lake) in Pahang, Malaysia — Malaysia's equivalent of the Loch Ness Monster. According to Orang Asli legend, the dragon was once a beautiful princess transformed into a serpentine guardian of the lake's mystical waters. The lake itself is a pristine body of water surrounded by ancient rainforest, and local folklore maintains that Seri Gumum is a protector rather than a menace. Fishermen speak of seeing a massive serpentine creature with golden scales breaching the surface, especially during storms and full moons. The dragon is considered the guardian of the lake's ecosystem — harming the lake's environment is believed to invoke its wrath. Local stories tell of the dragon surfacing during times of great change or crisis, serving as an omen of transformation
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seri_Gumum_Dragon

name: Seven Sisters
description: The Seven Sisters is a widespread Aboriginal Australian Dreaming story found across many language groups. The story tells of seven sisters who fled across the land and into the sky to escape a persistent pursuer, often a man named Wurrurrumbi or a hunter who wanted to take one of the sisters as his wife. As they fled, the sisters created landmarks, waterholes, and important sites across the Australian landscape. Finally they leaped into the sky, becoming the Pleiades star cluster. The pursuing man became the star Orion or the Moon, still chasing them across the heavens. In different regional versions, the sisters are associated with the arrival of the monsoon season or with ceremonies for girls' initiation. The story encodes practical knowledge about seasonal changes and the movements of celestial bodies
source: Australian Aboriginal dreamtime — the Seven Sisters (Pleiades) documented in Aboriginal oral tradition.

name: Zonbi
description: The Zonbi (or Zombi) is a malevolent spirit or reanimated corpse from Seychellois Creole folklore, related to similar figures found across the Indian Ocean and Caribbean islands. Unlike the Hollywood depiction of zombies as mindless undead, the Seychellois Zonbi is more closely associated with dark magic and witchcraft—a spirit or corpse animated by sorcery to serve a malevolent purpose. Seychellois Zonbi stories are typically less common than those of Soungoula or Tizan but speak to deep anxieties about death, the afterlife, and the misuse of spiritual power. In traditional belief, Zonbi are associated with abandoned historical sites, particularly those linked to the colonial era and the slave trade. The lingering trauma of slavery infuses Zonbi legends—the idea that those who died in bondage might return as restless spirits, or that dark magic practiced on plantations could reanimate the dead. Visiting abandoned colonial-era sites at night is said to increase the risk of encountering a Zonbi. These tales remind Seychellois of the lingering impact of their colonial past and the thin boundary between the living and the dead
source: Island Hopper Guides - Seychelles Folklore; The Creole Melting Pot; Seychelles Research Journal

name: Shadhavar
description: The Shadhavar is a legendary antelope-like creature from medieval Muslim bestiaries, thought to have originated in what is now Iraq. It resembles a gazelle or unicorn with a single hollow horn containing 42 hollow branches (72 in some versions, 74 in Flaubert's account). When wind passes through these flute-like cavities, the horn produces enchanting melodies so beautiful that all animals gather to listen. When played from the opposite side, the music turns into a mournful dirge that causes deep melancholy. In some stories, the Shadhavar stands six feet tall but appears gaunt, with dark patches on its face that resemble dripping tears. Al-Qazwini described it as native to the country of Rum (Byzantium), while al-Damiri and al-Mustawfi added embellishments, with the latter mistakenly calling it a carnivore
source: Al-Qazwini, Wonders of Creation; al-Damiri, Hayat al-Hayawan; al-Mustawfi; Middle East Eye

name: Shahmaran
description: Shahmaran (from Persian Shah-i-Maran, 'King of Snakes') is a mythical half-woman, half-snake creature revered in Azerbaijani, Turkish, and Kurdish folklore. She is the immortal queen of all serpents, possessing profound wisdom and magical healing powers. According to widespread legend, Shahmaran dwells in an underground realm beneath the ancient city of Tarsus, where intelligent and compassionate serpents live in peace. In Azerbaijani variants, her legend is known in Nakhchivan, Lankaran, and along the Araz River basin. The most famous tale tells of Cəmşab, a poor woodcutter who discovered Shahmaran's underground kingdom and lived with her for years, learning her secrets. After betraying her location to a sick king, Shahmaran was killed but arranged that her killer would die and her faithful friend would gain all the world's medical wisdom, becoming a legendary healer akin to Luqman In Azerbaijan folklore, this figure is known among the Azerbaijan people.
source: Azerbaijani/Persian mythology; the Shahmaran is a half-woman, half-snake deity.
